pass_a_gloss: And again in turn some, taking it that the names are by imposition and that they have no nature toward the underlying things of which they are names, consider that it differs nothing if someone should say: I revere the first God, or Zeus, or Zen, and if someone should affirm: I honour and receive the sun or Apollo, and the moon or Artemis, and the breath in the earth or Demeter, and as many other things as the wise ones of the Greeks say. Toward whom it must be said that there is also a certain most deep and withdrawn treatment about names, which the one who understands will see that, if the names were by imposition, the ones being called, demons or certain other powers unseen by us, would not have hearkened to those who mean them but name them as though the names were imposed; but now certain voicings and syllables, and namings announced with in-breathing or bareness or stretching or contraction, lead, perhaps by some nature unobservable to us, those being called. And if this holds so and the names are not by imposition, by no name must the first God be called except those with which the attendant and the prophets and the Saviour and our Lord himself name him, such as Sabaoth, Adonai, Shaddai, and again God of Abraham, God of Isaac and God of Jacob; for this, he says, is name age-long and remembrance to generations of generations. And not wonderful if the demons carry up their own namings onto the first God, so that as the first God it may be bowed down to. Which thing for the attendant who is with us and the prophets and the fullness of law, Christ, and his apostles is not of the fathers. And these things by necessity, so that no one may out-argue us or even to some amount stain our reckoning, we set beside; to which things one must hold the mind carefully, giving no place of side-attempt to the opposing ones.
pass_b_english: Again, some suppose that names are a matter of convention and have no natural bond with the things of which they are names. They think it makes no difference whether one says, “I worship the first God”, or “Zeus”, or “Zen”; or whether one declares, “I honour and acknowledge the sun”, or “Apollo”; “the moon”, or “Artemis”; “the spirit in the earth”, or “Demeter”; and whatever else the wise men of the Greeks say. To them we must reply that there is also a very deep and recondite study of names. Whoever understands it will see that if names were a matter of convention, the beings that are called on, demons or other powers invisible to us, would not answer those who mean them and call them by names as though the names had simply been laid down. As it is, certain sounds and syllables, and names spoken with a rough breathing or a smooth one, with a long vowel or a short, bring those who are called, perhaps by some nature that we cannot observe.

If this is so, and names are not a matter of convention, then the first God must be called by no other name than those by which the servant [Moses] and the prophets and our Saviour and Lord himself name him, such as Sabaoth, Adonai, Shaddai, and again, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob; “for this”, he says, “is an eternal name and a memorial for generation after generation” (Exodus 3:15). It is no wonder if the demons carry their own names over to the first God, so that they may be worshipped as the first God. That is not the ancestral way of our servant, or of the prophets, or of Christ, “the fulfilment of the law”, or of his apostles. We have set these things out because we had to, so that no one may outwit us with clever arguments, or defile our reasoning even a little. We must attend to them with care, giving our opponents no opening for attack.

choices.choice: 2026-11-11: retranslated in full from Koetschau (GCS 2, ch. 46); the old English was a digest: it put in an argument about 'mind' and 'soul' as names, 'Zeus names a demon rejoicing in stolen honour' and Wisdom of Solomon 9:15 (which belongs to ch. 47), and dropped the study of names, the breathings and vowel lengths, Sabaoth, Adonai, Shaddai and Exodus 3:15.
'the servant [Moses]': identification supplied in brackets at first mention; the second 'our servant' is left as Origen writes it.
'0v0ματα' read as 'ὀνόματα'; 'διαφέρει»' as 'διαφέρειν'; 'φασὶ»' as 'φασίν'; 'οἷον Σαβαὼθ., ᾿Αδωναὶϊ' as 'Σαβαώθ, Ἀδωναΐ'.
Singular verb with neuter plural 'τὰ δαιμόνια' as subject: 'so that they [the demons] may be worshipped as the first God'.
